sections.html:
Northwest of Tucson, Marana is a growing town full of newer subdivisions, so ask first whether your house belongs to an HOA. Then choose a route, an agent listing or a direct cash sale, and clear the HOA, tax and title items that usually hold up closings.

The town's population was estimated at 65,523 on July 1, 2025, up 26.2 percent from the April 2020 base. Owners occupy 83.7 percent of homes, and the median owner-occupied home is worth $413,800. Median gross rent is $1,818 and median household income is $112,606, across 21,767 households. The mean commute is 27.7 minutes, so mention highway access in your listing.

Listing puts the house in front of the most buyers. A cash sale can close with no lender appraisal, which leaves the schedule mostly to you and the buyer's title company. Before you accept an offer, line up the following:

  • HOA name, manager and a recent assessment statement
  • Payoff letters for each loan or lien
  • Utility, solar lease or battery lease contacts, if any
  • Records of permitted work such as pools, casitas and patio covers
  • The current Pima County or Pinal County tax bill

Marana lies mostly in Pima County, with a small piece in Pinal County, and stretches along Interstate 10 from the county line to the Tucson city limits. It covers about 121 square miles among the Tortolita, Santa Catalina and Tucson mountains and includes the Dove Mountain area. Look at your tax statement to see which county bills you, because that decides your due dates.

The school district also depends on the address. Most of the town is in the Marana Unified School District, which serves grades preK to 12 from an office at 11279 W. Grier Road. Flowing Wells Unified covers the far southeastern edge, and the Pinal County portion is served by Red Rock Elementary and Santa Cruz Valley Union High School districts. Confirm the district with a street address search before you list.

Flood risk varies lot by lot. A buyer, lender or insurer will want to know whether the property sits in a mapped FEMA floodplain, so look up your parcel before you list and keep any flood insurance paperwork handy.

A house in an unincorporated area rather than inside town limits falls under A.R.S. 33-422 when the seller offers five or fewer parcels other than subdivided land. The law calls for a written affidavit of disclosure at least seven days before transfer, covering legal and physical access, road maintenance, floodplain status, utilities, wells and septic systems, and it gives the buyer a five-day right to rescind.

If the house is in a planned community, the HOA sets part of your timeline. Under A.R.S. 33-1806, once you accept an offer in a community of 50 or more properties you notify the association, and the association has ten days to send the buyer its bylaws, declaration, recent board minutes, budget, financial reports, assessment amounts and any unpaid lien or open violation. In smaller communities the seller delivers the information within the same ten days.

The association collects these at the close of escrow and cannot charge them twice for one transaction. The buyer signs a statement at closing acknowledging the community's covenants and assessments. Ask the HOA manager for the package early, because an unpaid assessment shows up as a lien that comes out of your proceeds.

Ask the Town's Development Services Center for the permit history on your address, especially for pools, casitas, solar and garage work, and close any open permits before a buyer's inspector finds them.

A short-term rental in Marana requires:

  • A Town business license for the rental
  • A valid Transaction Privilege Tax number from the state
  • Registration with the Pima County Assessor
  • A neighbor notification attestation emailed to licensing@maranaaz.gov before the rental start date
  • Annual renewal, with an invoice mailed 30 days before expiration, and updates to the Town within 10 days of any change

If you ran the house as a short-term rental, hand the buyer the license and registration details. Anyone planning to rent should ask the Town's licensing staff what a fresh application requires.

Most Marana deeds are recorded with the Pima County Recorder, which charges a flat $30 recording fee under A.R.S. 11-475, plus a $5 fee to return documents submitted improperly. The Affidavit of Property Value form comes from the Arizona Department of Revenue. State law requires the affidavit with a transfer deed unless the deed shows an exemption (A.R.S. 11-1133). For the small part of Marana in Pinal County, the Pinal County Recorder charges $30 for any document, and that fee already covers the affidavit of property value.

Pima County mails its bills by the end of September. For the 2026 year, the dates are:

  • The full year is due by December 31, 2026.
  • The second half is due March 1, 2027 and delinquent May 3, 2027.

The first half is due each October 1 and turns delinquent in early November. The Pima Treasurer's office takes online payments at to.pima.gov or by phone at 520-724-8341, and charges a 1.95 percent convenience fee on card payments with a $1.95 minimum, or $0.50 for an eCheck. Address changes for tax bills go through the Pima County Assessor.

Pinal County parcels follow Pinal's own schedule, with the first half delinquent after 5 p.m. on November 1 and the second half after May 1. Ask your escrow officer to confirm what remains unpaid and how the year will be split at closing.

With an offer in hand, a title company opens escrow. It checks the record for liens, requests payoff letters, divides the year's tax between you and the buyer, and prepares the deed and the affidavit. If an HOA is involved, the title company also coordinates the resale package and any lien statement, and the association's fees come out at the close of escrow.

Cash buyers remove the loan from the chain, so nobody waits on an appraisal or underwriting. Your remaining tasks are the same as in any sale: leave the house in the agreed condition, hand over keys, remotes and any solar or battery lease paperwork, and keep a copy of the settlement statement. Check the HOA statement and the tax bill once more a few days before closing, because those two items cause most late surprises.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Marana house with an HOA lien or unpaid assessment?
faqs.a: Yes. The HOA's resale statement lists any unpaid assessment lien, and your escrow officer can pay it from your proceeds if you agree. Ask the association for its statement early, since it has ten days after notice of a pending sale to deliver the resale package to the buyer.

faqs.q: How much does it cost to record a deed for a Marana property?
faqs.a: The Pima County Recorder lists $30 per document, and the Pinal County Recorder lists the same $30. The Affidavit of Property Value is required unless the deed shows an exemption. Your escrow or title company normally pays and files these at closing.

faqs.q: Is Marana in Pima County or Pinal County?
faqs.a: Mostly Pima County, with a small portion in Pinal County. Pima County bills most Marana homes, while the Pinal County Treasurer bills parcels in the Pinal portion. Look at your tax statement to see which county issues your bill and which due dates apply.

faqs.q: When is the next Pima County property tax payment due for a Marana home?
faqs.a: The second half is due March 1, 2027 and delinquent May 3, 2027. Paying the full year by December 31, 2026 avoids interest accrued after November 1.

Yes, with a Town business license. The owner needs a Transaction Privilege Tax number, Pima County Assessor registration and a neighbor notification attestation before the rental starts. Licenses renew each year, and changes must be reported to the Town within 10 days.
